parts.note: reads as a ruler of the skies, but means a royal name (George IV's wife) that is also the title of a song, an air

explanation.surface: Someone asks who rules the skies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air' suggests the sky; here it is a tune. The name belonged to Queen Caroline and is also the title of songs.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of a British queen consort that is also the title of popular songs, airs.

clue.text: "His silver hairs will purchase us a good opinion" (J. Caesar)

definitions.text: "His silver hairs will purchase us a good opinion" (J. Caesar)

parts.words: "His silver hairs will purchase us a good opinion" (J. Caesar)
parts.note: in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar, Metellus says this of the old Roman orator whom the conspirators want on their side

explanation.walkthrough: Metellus Cimber speaks the line in Act 2 Scene 1, urging that the elder statesman be recruited to lend the plot respectability.
explanation.definitionFit: The great Roman orator whose age and standing the conspirators hoped would win them respect.

clue.text: Wound up a slippery fellow in a state of insolvency

indicators.note: the slippery creature is placed inside the word for being in debt

parts.note: being in the red means owing money
an eel is a slippery creature

explanation.surface: A slippery debtor who has gone broke is reeled in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wound up' looks like 'liquidated', fitting the insolvency, but it means wound in on a reel, as an angler does.
explanation.definitionFit: Wound a line in on a reel, as an angler does.

parts.note: Bishop Hugh, burnt at Oxford in 1555, told Ridley 'we shall this day light such a candle' as would never be put out

explanation.walkthrough: The bishop at the stake in 1555 spoke of lighting a candle, by God's grace, in England that would never be put out.
explanation.definitionFit: The Protestant bishop and martyr who spoke of lighting a candle as he burned.

clue.text: What's the sense in refusal to go to America ?

parts.note: a refusal is a no
US is short for the United States, America

explanation.surface: Someone questions the wisdom of refusing a trip to America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To go to' simply places the two pieces side by side. The definition is British informal for common sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal British word, from Greek for mind, meaning practical good sense.

parts.note: looks like overalls, but means a card suit whose name is also that of a digging tool used for work

explanation.walkthrough: 'Suit' suggests clothing; it is one of the four suits in a pack of cards, named after a digging tool.
explanation.definitionFit: A suit in a pack of cards that shares its name with the garden tool used for digging work.

definitions.meaning: a wide, flat grassland, as in North America
a hangover cure of raw egg, Worcestershire sauce and seasoning carries this name

explanation.surface: Someone describes an ordinary, unremarkable kind of oyster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain' looks like an adjective for the oyster; it is a noun, the grassland. The oyster is a raw-egg drink, not a shellfish.
explanation.definitionFit: A grassland plain, and the raw-egg hangover drink named after an oyster.

indicators.note: double means the share word is written twice in a row

parts.note: a divi is a dividend, the interest paid on shares

explanation.surface: A leather works pays its investors twice the usual return.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like a factory, fitting a tannery, but it is a tropical tree whose pods are used in tanning; 'pays' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A tropical American tree whose curled pods yield tannin for leather making.

definitions.meaning: anxious tension about what will happen
a delay or temporary stopping, as when a payment is held back

explanation.surface: Someone asks what the thrill is about and is told a robbery is happening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold-up' suggests a robbery; here it means a delay or suspension.
explanation.definitionFit: Tense uncertainty, and a temporary stopping or deferral.

clue.text: Joe Miller put Smith in the shade

definitions.meaning: an old, stale joke, after the eighteenth-century jest book 'Joe Miller's Jests'
Longfellow's village smithy stands under a spreading tree of this kind, which shades him

explanation.surface: A man named Joe Miller made a rival called Smith look inferior.
explanation.walkthrough: Both names look like people. 'Joe Miller' is old slang for a stale joke, and Longfellow's poem begins 'Under a spreading ... tree The village smithy stands'.
explanation.definitionFit: A stale old joke, and the tree that shades Longfellow's village blacksmith.

clue.text: So a chiseller works his way to the head of the table?

definitions.text: So a chiseller works his way to the head of the table?

parts.words: So a chiseller works his way to the head of the table?
parts.note: a sculptor cuts stone with a chisel, and the person at the head of a dinner table slices the roast

explanation.surface: A swindler schemes his way into the top seat.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'chiseller' is slang for a cheat, but here it is a sculptor; the head of the table is where the meat is sliced at a family meal.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb for what a sculptor does to stone and what the host does to the Sunday joint.

clue.text: Family that sounds to be sitting on the muzzle of a gun

indicators.note: sounds signals that the gun part is heard, not spelt, giving the family name

parts.words: sitting on the muzzle of a gun
parts.note: the foresight is the sight fixed at the muzzle end of a gun barrel

explanation.surface: A family seems to live perched at the end of a gun barrel.
explanation.walkthrough: The family is Galsworthy's in 'The Forsyte Saga'; 'that' and 'to be' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: The family of John Galsworthy's novel sequence about a wealthy Victorian clan.

parts.note: J. Daw is the Jackdaw of the Ingoldsby Legends, who stole a cardinal's ring in a French cathedral city

explanation.surface: A notorious jewel thief's hideout is being named.
explanation.walkthrough: J. Daw is a jackdaw: in R. H. Barham's poem 'The Jackdaw of Rheims' the bird steals the cardinal's ring.
explanation.definitionFit: The French cathedral city where Barham's thieving jackdaw lived.

clue.text: What's the problem of a poet's breakfast:

definitions.text: What's the problem of a poet's breakfast:

parts.words: What's the problem of a poet's breakfast:
parts.note: the oat dish a poet might eat is a problem for poets because nothing in English rhymes with its name

explanation.surface: Someone wonders what troubles a poet at the breakfast table.
explanation.walkthrough: The problem is not the taste: the word for this breakfast food famously has no rhyme in English. The scan prints a question mark where the feed has a colon.
explanation.definitionFit: An oatmeal breakfast dish whose name has no rhyme, so it troubles a poet.

parts.note: a town crier rings a bell and barks out announcements, asking passers-by whether they know the news

explanation.surface: Someone asks if you know a lunatic bell-ringer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barking' looks like British slang for mad, or a dog; it is shouting out notices. 'D'ye ken' is Scots for 'do you know?'
explanation.definitionFit: A town crier who rings a handbell before shouting out the news.

parts.note: a lawn is green, and lawn is also a fine linen used for sleeves, giving the title of an old English tune

explanation.surface: Someone asks about a band playing on the grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lawn' is grass, so green, and also the fine linen of a bishop's sleeves; together they give the Tudor song.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous old English tune whose title joins a grass colour with the parts of a garment.

clue.text: Among top fighter pilots Hill was a hero

indicators.note: among places the name inside the word for the best airmen

parts.note: aces are fighter pilots with many kills
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pilot named Hill was a hero among the leading fighter aces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Was' is a link. Hill looks like a pilot's surname; the hero is the Greek warrior of the Trojan War.
explanation.definitionFit: The great Greek warrior of Homer's Iliad, champion at Troy.

parts.note: local means on the spot, and currency means money, giving payment made there and then

explanation.walkthrough: 'Local currency' suggests a nation's money; read it as money paid on the spot, immediate payment.
explanation.definitionFit: Payment in money made immediately on delivery rather than on credit.

parts.note: the landscape gardener Lancelot Brown was nicknamed for the word he used about the potential of estates; 'singular' points to that one-word nickname

explanation.surface: A man called Brown had remarkable gifts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singular' looks like 'remarkable', but it means the nickname is the singular of the plural answer: 'Capability' Brown, the 18th-century English landscape gardener.
explanation.definitionFit: Plural of the nickname of Lancelot Brown, the landscape designer; the word means aptitudes.

clue.text: Theirs was a colourful show about the Pole

definitions.text: Theirs was a colourful show about the Pole

parts.words: Theirs was a colourful show about the Pole
parts.note: a hairdresser for men hangs a red-and-white striped pole outside the shop

explanation.surface: A troupe staged a vivid display about a Polish man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' looks like a Polish person, or the North Pole; it is the striped pole outside a men's hair shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Men's hairdressers, whose shops display the red-and-white striped pole.

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
an estuary is a river mouth

explanation.surface: Someone asks if an old river port is still a town, and is told it is.
explanation.walkthrough: The playful 'Still is' says the place is not 'former' at all: it is a Devon town at the mouth of the river Exe.
explanation.definitionFit: A seaside resort in Devon, England, at the mouth of the river Exe.

clue.text: The sage takes Diana in a river-craft

indicators.note: in places the short name inside the boat word

parts.note: a punt is a flat-bottomed river boat
Di is short for Diana

explanation.surface: A wise man takes a woman called Diana out on the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Takes' is a link. A punt is a flat boat pushed with a pole on English rivers such as the Cam.
explanation.definitionFit: An expert or learned authority who gives opinions, from the Hindi word for a learned man.

clue.text: Bob, her father has reached the peaks

parts.note: a bob was a shilling in old British money, abbreviated s
taken as written
pa is father

explanation.surface: Bob says that a woman's father has climbed to the summits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a name; it is old British slang for a shilling, written s. The definition describes the Himalayan people, one of whom, Tenzing, reached Everest's summit in 1953.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the Himalayan people famed as mountain guides who climb the highest summits.

clue.text: Form of lantern I don't take outside

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a form of something is a version of it with its parts rearranged, so these letters are reshaped

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A medicine label in the shape of a lantern warns against outdoor use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Form of' reworks LANTERN into NTERNAL, set after I. Medicine marked for use inside the body is not to be taken outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Something internal belongs inside the body, the reverse of what is meant to be used outside it.

parts.note: matutinal means of the morning, abbreviated AM
a shrub is a bush

explanation.surface: A bush at dawn waits for the coming of spring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' looks like the season, but it is a sudden leap: an attacker in hiding waits to spring on the victim.
explanation.definitionFit: Lying in wait to leap out on a victim is a surprise attack from hiding.

parts.note: a call to a man to sing high: the word for this voice comes from Italian for high, and a man's falsetto voice is so named

explanation.surface: A choirmaster urges a male singer to sing louder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sing up' means louder; here it means sing high, in the male high voice whose name comes from Italian 'alto', high.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest adult male singing voice, named from Italian for high.

clue.text: This hall should have been built plumb

definitions.text: This hall should have been built plumb

parts.words: This hall should have been built plumb
parts.note: ... is a London market; plumb, from Latin plumbum, is the heavy metal lead, so the hall should be made of it

explanation.surface: A builder complains that a hall was put up crooked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plumb' looks like 'upright', but plumbum is Latin for lead; Leadenhall is a historic covered market in the City of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Made of lead, the metal named in Latin plumbum, as in the London market name Leadenhall.

clue.text: Practised swimmer seen to be in difficulties

definitions.meaning: a flatfish, which naturally swims well
to struggle clumsily or be out of one's depth

explanation.surface: An expert swimmer is spotted struggling in the water.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a swimmer in trouble; the two senses are a fish and a verb for struggling.
explanation.definitionFit: A flatfish, an expert at swimming; also to struggle or stumble helplessly.

parts.note: looks like the continental watershed in the Rockies, but means the split in the Western Church of 1378 to 1417, with rival popes

explanation.walkthrough: The Great Divide is a mountain watershed in North America; the Great Western split saw two or three popes at once.
explanation.definitionFit: A split within a church or group, as in the medieval Great Western one.

parts.note: the legendary African king of the ballad and Tennyson's poem who wedded a beggar maid

explanation.surface: A man wed a woman who lived on charity.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted words echo the ballad of the king who fell in love with a beggar maid, told also in Tennyson's 'The Beggar Maid'.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary king who wedded the beggar maid Penelophon.
